strengths: The paper studies a simple, lightweight architectural intervention that is easy to integrate into actor-critic agents and appears to add little wall-clock overhead.
The empirical scope is unusually broad, spanning off-policy and on-policy algorithms, continuous and discrete control, offline-to-online learning, multitask learning, and several robot morphologies.
The results generally show consistent improvements in early learning and often final return across many tasks, algorithms, and hyperparameter variations, using multiple seeds.

Ablations compare actor-only, critic-only, and joint placement; vary the simplex dimensions; and include alternative structured representations such as CReLU, Gumbel straight-through, and vector quantization.
Representation and optimization diagnostics provide useful hypotheses connecting SEM to feature rank, sparsity, bounded feature norms, TD error, and critic disagreement.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: simplicial embeddings are an existing component, and the paper acknowledges that TD-MPC2 already constrains encoder outputs using SEM. The primary contribution is therefore a broad empirical application to additional actor-critic pipelines rather than a substantially new method.

The formal result is not valid as stated. Equation 5 only indicates tracking of a moving optimum; it does not establish that non-stationarity causes covariance deflation, decreases ReLU activation probabilities, or increases neuron dormancy. Those crucial steps are asserted without assumptions or derivation, so Theorem 1 and the claimed mechanism are unsupported.

The evaluation relies heavily on learning-curve inspection. It lacks numerical summaries of final performance and sample efficiency, confidence intervals or clearly specified uncertainty estimates, and statistical comparisons across tasks. Aggregate normalization procedures are also insufficiently documented.

Important controls are missing. SEM changes the penultimate architecture relative to the Linear-ReLU baseline, but there is no carefully parameter- and capacity-matched softmax/group-normalization control, making it difficult to attribute gains specifically to simplicial geometry rather than bottleneck size, normalization, or altered parameterization.

The mechanistic evidence is correlational: higher rank, greater sparsity, smaller TD error, and improved return occur together, but no intervention demonstrates that preventing representation collapse causes the performance gains. The CIFAR-10 label-permutation experiment is also a weak proxy for actor-critic non-stationarity.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the paper's claim: the appendix does not clearly report the chosen L, V, and temperature for every experiment, implementation details for several secondary benchmarks are sparse, hardware and timing methodology are omitted, and no code release is identified.

There are presentation and consistency problems, including an Atari figure legend referring to FastTD3 although the experiment uses PPO, Figure 20 plotting G1 tasks while its caption says 16 H1 tasks, and Figures 20 and 21 appearing to duplicate the same curves while claiming different task counts. These errors reduce confidence in the experimental accounting.

strengths: The proposed intervention is simple and lightweight: a group-wise softmax can be inserted into existing actor networks without auxiliary objectives or major algorithmic changes.
The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering several actor-critic algorithms and continuous-control, multitask, offline-to-online, and pixel-based environments.
The paper includes useful ablations over actor versus critic placement, simplex dimensions, environment count, replay-buffer size, batch size, and selected FastTD3 design choices.
Per-task learning curves and six-seed continuous-control experiments provide more evidence than aggregate results alone.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited. The simplicial embedding itself is taken from prior work, and the paper acknowledges that TD-MPC2 already constrains RL encoder outputs using essentially this mechanism. The main contribution is therefore an empirical application to additional actor-critic architectures rather than a new method or principle.

The claimed formal analysis is not valid as a theorem. Crucial steps—non-stationarity causing covariance deflation, reducing ReLU activation probabilities, and increasing dormancy—are asserted rather than derived. Moreover, unit mass of each simplex block does not bound feature covariance away from zero: all observations can map to the same nonzero vector while covariance is exactly zero. Equation 7 also requires unstated assumptions and conflates feature energy with centered covariance.

The mechanistic claims are consequently much stronger than the evidence. Higher rank, lower TD error, and better returns are correlated measurements on only two selected tasks; they do not establish that SEM improves performance by preventing collapse rather than these diagnostics changing as a consequence of faster learning.

The architectural comparison is confounded. The baseline uses Linear-ReLU-Linear while the SEM model uses SEM-Linear, but parameter counts, output dimensions, initialization, and matched-capacity controls are not reported. Comparisons against simple bounded or normalized activations, plain group-wise softmax controls, and other directly relevant normalization methods are missing.

Statistical reporting is inadequate for the breadth of the claims. The paper primarily presents smoothed curves without numerical summary tables, confidence intervals with clearly defined construction, significance tests, or aggregate uncertainty across tasks. Normalized-return definitions and sample-efficiency metrics such as AUC or steps-to-threshold are not specified.

Reproducibility is weak: no code or artifact is identified, and important SEM details—including the final L, V, and temperature choices across experiment families—are incomplete. Hardware and measurement protocol for runtime are also absent. The claim of no runtime loss is not established by Table 2, where SEM is slower on some tasks and no uncertainty is provided.

There are numerous internal inconsistencies that reduce confidence in the evaluation. The text calls the Atari evaluation 'Atari-10' while reporting 27 games; Figure 19 labels its baseline as FastTD3 although the experiment is described as PPO; Figures 20 and 21 appear duplicated or mislabeled; and task counts and robot labels disagree across captions and surrounding text.

The paper describes Booster T1 as a real-robot benchmark and invokes sim-to-real validation, but its own appendix states that the submitted experiments were conducted in simulation. Thus the manuscript provides no real-robot evidence for SEM.

The CIFAR-10 label-permutation experiment is a weak proxy for actor-critic non-stationarity and lacks enough methodological and uncertainty information to support the general conclusion drawn from it.

Overall, the extensive experiments are promising, but limited novelty, invalid theoretical arguments, architectural confounds, incomplete statistical analysis, and substantial reporting inconsistencies prevent the central claims from meeting the standard of a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The empirical study is broad and generally convincing: SEM improves multiple off-policy and on-policy agents across humanoid control, IsaacGym, Atari, multitask RL, and offline-to-online RL, with per-task curves and multiple seeds. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/6a27128cf082409185f60c58f0e16a36/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The intervention is simple, differentiable, and practically attractive. Reported wall-clock times indicate that its sample-efficiency gains do not introduce meaningful runtime overhead.

The paper includes useful ablations over actor versus critic placement, simplex dimensions, capacity, core FastTD3 design choices, and alternative regularizers, together with representation and optimization diagnostics that offer plausible insight into the observed gains.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate: simplicial embeddings are an existing technique, and the related-work section acknowledges that TD-MPC2 already constrains encoder outputs in this way. The main novelty is therefore the extensive actor-critic investigation rather than a new representation method.

The formal analysis does not substantiate its stated theorem. The proof asserts, rather than derives, that non-stationarity causes covariance deflation and reduced activation probabilities. Moreover, simplex normalization does not ensure that representation covariance is bounded away from zero, since all inputs could map to the same simplex point. Thus, the proposed causal account should be treated as an empirical hypothesis rather than a theorem.

Quantitative reporting relies heavily on plotted aggregate curves. The paper lacks consolidated AUC/final-return tables, uncertainty summaries or statistical tests, and a precise description of return normalization, making effect sizes and consistency harder to assess rigorously.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite the paper's claim: the tables omit central SEM settings such as L, V, and temperature for the different experimental suites, as well as several training-budget and evaluation details. No code or artifact availability statement is provided.

The real-robot discussion is potentially misleading: the reported Booster T1 experiment appears to evaluate simulation performance using a setup previously transferred to hardware, rather than demonstrating a new real-robot deployment of SEM.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically important limitation of highly parallel actor–critic methods and proposes an exceptionally simple intervention: a differentiable group-wise softmax bottleneck that adds little computational or implementation complexity.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, spanning FastTD3, FastTD3-SimBaV2, FastSAC, PPO, and FQL; state- and pixel-based observations; continuous and discrete control; multitask learning; and offline-to-online adaptation.

Results generally show consistent improvements in early learning and final return. The use of six seeds for continuous-control experiments, per-task curves, IQM aggregation for Atari, and confidence intervals strengthens the evidence.

The paper includes extensive ablations over actor versus critic placement, layer placement, simplex dimensions, environment parallelism, replay and batch sizes, and FastTD3 components. Comparisons with quantization, C-ReLU, normalization, reset, pruning, MoE, and other regularizers help isolate the value of SEM.

Representation and optimization diagnostics—effective rank, feature norms, sparsity, TD error, critic disagreement, and Cramer distance—provide useful empirical clues about why the method works. The authors also appropriately report the negative aggregate result for value-based PQN.
The presentation is generally accessible, and the wall-clock measurements support the claim that SEM largely preserves the speed of the underlying agents.
weaknesses: The core architectural mechanism is not novel: simplicial embeddings are taken from prior work, and the paper itself notes that TD-MPC2 already constrains encoder outputs using a similar mechanism. The main novelty is therefore an extensive empirical study and application to fast actor–critic agents rather than a new algorithmic principle.

The stated formal result is not established. The proof merely asserts that non-stationary drift causes covariance deflation and lowers ReLU activation probabilities; these conclusions do not follow from the tracking-error recursion. Likewise, simplex normalization prevents feature norms from vanishing but does not prevent covariance collapse, since every input could map to the same simplex point. Thus, strong causal claims about preventing collapse are unsupported.

The CIFAR-10 experiment with periodically permuted labels is a weak proxy for RL bootstrapping and conflates abrupt contradictory target changes with the structured non-stationarity induced by an evolving policy. The diagnostic correlations in RL do not establish that improved rank or sparsity causes the performance gains.

Results are presented almost entirely as plots, without numerical tables of aggregate scores, effect sizes, probability-of-improvement estimates, or statistical comparisons. This makes it difficult to quantify consistency across tasks and to assess claims such as improved asymptotic performance.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite the reproducibility statement. The SEM temperature and many benchmark-specific SEM settings are not systematically reported; configurations for FQL, MTBench, FastSAC, and SimBaV2 are underspecified; parameter-count matching is unclear; and the manuscript contains only a placeholder source-code link.

Several reporting inconsistencies reduce confidence: Figure 28's caption names FastSAC while its legend shows FastTD3-SimBaV2; Figures 31 and 32 appear duplicated and have inconsistent task/robot descriptions; and the text misreferences the MTBench panel. The Booster T1 experiment is simulation-only, so references to a real-robot benchmark should not be interpreted as a new physical deployment.
The ethics statement is perfunctory for work targeting humanoid and robotic control, and does not discuss safety, sim-to-real failure modes, or possible resource costs.

strengths: The empirical study is unusually broad, covering several actor–critic algorithms and continuous-control, multitask, offline-to-online, and pixel-based benchmarks; many reported improvements are substantial and consistent. SEM is lightweight, differentiable, easy to integrate, and appears to preserve approximately the same wall-clock performance as the underlying agents.

The paper includes useful actor-versus-critic placement studies, layer-wise and dimensionality ablations, representation diagnostics, and comparisons with numerous regularization or plasticity interventions.
The per-task curves expose heterogeneous outcomes rather than presenting only aggregate scores, and the negative PQN result appropriately limits the claimed generality.
weaknesses: The formal centerpiece is unsound. Theorem 1 is not proved: after deriving a local tracking-error recursion, the argument simply asserts that non-stationarity causes covariance deflation, lowers ReLU activation probabilities, and increases dormancy. None of these implications follows from Equation 4, and counterexamples are easy to construct. The statement that the drift term is zero when consecutive data distributions agree also ignores possible target-function drift.

The novelty is limited. SEM is an existing group-wise softmax representation, and the paper acknowledges that prior RL systems such as TD-MPC2 already constrain encodings in this manner. The main contribution is consequently an extensive application study rather than a new method or valid theoretical insight.

The proposed causal explanation is not established. Higher effective rank, lower TD error, sparsity, and return are measured on the same trained agents and are largely correlational; several quantities are also mechanically affected by the simplex transformation. There is no intervention showing that preventing rank loss or dormancy mediates the performance gain.

Architectural comparisons are insufficiently controlled. SEM changes the penultimate computation, dimensionality/capacity through L×V, and in some descriptions replaces a Linear–ReLU block. Matching parameter counts, output dimensions, depth, activation statistics, and compute against plain softmax or other bounded activations is necessary to isolate the claimed simplicial inductive bias.

Evaluation and reporting are less rigorous than their scale suggests. Many appendix comparisons show only mean curves without uncertainty or formal paired statistics; hyperparameters and normalization details are incomplete, including the temperature and the selected L and V for most settings. The manuscript also contains inconsistent benchmark/figure references and an unresolved source-code placeholder, weakening reproducibility.

The strongest ablations and alternative-baseline comparisons are concentrated on five closely related HumanoidBench tasks that were also used to choose SEM configurations. It is unclear whether hyperparameter selection transfers without tuning to the broader evaluation, creating a risk of selection bias.

Several claims are overstated: SEM does not consistently improve all examined regimes, the wall-clock table sometimes shows a measurable slowdown, and per-task curves include ties and regressions. The ethical statement is also perfunctory given the discussion of real-robot transfer and large-scale computational use.

strengths: The paper identifies an important practical problem: improving the sample efficiency of high-throughput actor–critic methods without sacrificing their wall-clock advantages.

The intervention is exceptionally simple and broadly applicable: a group-wise softmax constrains latent features to a product of simplices, requiring neither auxiliary objectives nor additional networks.
The empirical study is unusually broad, covering FastTD3, FastTD3-SimBaV2, FastSAC, PPO, and FQL across humanoid control, Isaac Gym, Atari, multitask robotics, and offline-to-online RL.

Results consistently show improved early learning and often higher final performance across multiple actor–critic algorithms and task families. Most continuous-control experiments use six seeds, and the paper reports uncertainty intervals.
The authors provide extensive ablations covering actor versus critic placement, simplex dimensions, layer placement, environment count, replay-buffer and batch size, and key FastTD3 components.

Comparisons against discretization and regularization alternatives—including vector quantization, Gumbel straight-through, C-ReLU, feature normalization, spectral normalization, resets, ReDo, pruning, and MoE variants—substantially strengthen the empirical case.

Representation and optimization diagnostics, including effective rank, feature norms, sparsity, TD error, and critic disagreement, offer useful evidence beyond returns and help motivate the proposed mechanism.
The paper appropriately reports the negative aggregate result for value-based PQN rather than presenting SEM as universally beneficial.
Measured runtimes suggest that SEM preserves approximately the same training speed as the baseline, supporting its practical appeal.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental: simplicial embeddings are an existing architectural component, and prior RL systems such as TD-MPC2 already use simplex-constrained encodings. The main contribution is therefore the empirical study and adaptation to actor–critic networks rather than a new representation method.

The formal result is not established by the supplied proof. The argument assumes, rather than derives, that non-stationary drift causes covariance deflation and reduces ReLU activation probabilities. Distributional drift does not necessarily imply a nonzero gradient at the previous minimizer, nor does it necessarily decrease rank or increase dormancy. Consequently, the stated theorem and mechanistic claims should be substantially weakened or proved under explicit assumptions.

Several causal statements are stronger than the experiments support. Correlations between SEM, effective rank, and improved returns do not establish that preventing representation collapse causes the performance gains; bounded scale, altered optimization, or changed network capacity could also explain them.

The statistical reporting is weaker than the breadth of experimentation suggests. Most central results appear only as aggregate learning curves, without numerical tables of final return, area under the learning curve, confidence intervals, or paired significance tests. Per-task plots also reveal heterogeneous effects that aggregate curves can obscure.

Architecture-matched controls are insufficiently documented. Replacing a baseline linear/ReLU block with SEM can change dimensionality and parameter count, while the paper argues that performance depends strongly on the product L×V. Comparisons controlling exactly for width, parameter count, activation normalization, and temperature would better isolate the geometric contribution.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite the reproducibility claim. The appendix omits or under-specifies important SEM settings such as temperature and task-specific L/V choices, as well as complete training and evaluation protocols for several benchmark-algorithm combinations. The source-code reference is also not concretely available in the manuscript.

The wall-clock claim is supported by only five task-level measurements, with no hardware specification, repeated timing uncertainty, or end-to-end throughput analysis. These numbers justify 'similar runtime' more readily than 'no loss in runtime speed.'

There are multiple presentation inconsistencies: MTBench is incorrectly referenced as Figure 10 right instead of Figure 11 right, an additional-experiment caption labels plotted G1 tasks as H1 tasks, and the value-based aggregate caption states 18 games although the text and per-game figure state 28. These errors reduce confidence in experimental bookkeeping.
The ethics statement is overly dismissive for work involving humanoid control and sim-to-real framing; a brief discussion of deployment safety and misuse would be more appropriate.
